prayer.text: Saint Ferdinand III of Castile, pray for us.

cues.text: A Boy King Between Two Crowns
Ferdinand was born around 1198 near Salamanca, the son of King Alfonso IX of Leon and Berenguela of Castile, whose own father was king of Castile in his own right.
When the Castilian throne fell vacant, Berenguela renounced her claim in her son's favor.
Ferdinand was proclaimed king of Castile in 1217, not yet twenty years old, despite a father who briefly took up arms against his own son's succession.
Father and son eventually reconciled, and in 1230, on Alfonso IX's death, Ferdinand inherited Leon as well, permanently uniting the two kingdoms his mother's diplomacy had first joined.

He governed from the start with a caution unusual in a warrior-king of his age, surrounding himself with wise counselors and, by his own often-repeated words, fearing the curse of a single wronged widow more than an army of enemies.
The Reconquest
Ferdinand spent much of his reign extending Christian rule across southern Spain, capturing Cordoba in 1236.
He restored its great mosque, built centuries earlier under Muslim rule, to Christian worship, then took Seville in 1248 after a long siege, the crowning conquest of his career.
He fasted and prayed before his campaigns, and chroniclers close to his court describe a king who fought less for personal glory.
They portray him as seeking the restoration of Christian order to lands lost centuries before, treating conquered populations, on the whole, with a degree of legal protection unusual for the period.

Alongside the sword, he built: the Cathedral of Burgos rose under his patronage, and he supported the University of Salamanca, endowing it with the resources to become one of medieval Europe's great centers of learning.
A King's Ordinary Holiness
Ferdinand's sanctity, as the sources that survive describe it, showed itself less in any single dramatic act than in the daily discipline of a ruler who treated justice as itself a form of prayer.
He was associated with the Franciscan Third Order, wearing the plain habit of a Franciscan tertiary beneath his royal dress.
He promoted the use and compilation of important legal texts, including the Fuero Juzgo, in his realms.
Widowed by the death of his first wife, Beatrice of Swabia, in 1236, he married again.
By his two marriages, he left behind fifteen children, among them his heir Alfonso X, later called 'the Wise,' who would carry his father's work of consolidation forward.
Death and an Unexpected Missouri Legacy
Ferdinand died at Seville on May 30, 1252, after a long illness, and was buried at his own request in the plain habit of the Franciscan Third Order.
He was buried in the cathedral he had helped restore to Christian worship; his body is still venerated there today, enclosed in a gold and crystal casket.
More than five centuries later, French colonists on the far side of the Atlantic named a small settlement in Spanish Upper Louisiana after him — St. Ferdinand, in what is now Florissant, Missouri.
The parish that grew there became, in the early nineteenth century, the home base of St. Rose Philippine Duchesne , whose own convent stood only steps from the church that still bears his name.
Legacy
Pope Clement X canonized Ferdinand in 1671, four centuries after his death, recognizing a king whose warfare never eclipsed his justice and whose justice never hardened into cruelty.
He was a first cousin of another canonized medieval monarch, St. Louis IX of France.
This proves that holiness on a throne, however rare, was not a single accident of thirteenth-century Europe.
It ran, at least occasionally, in the blood of families willing to let it.
We recognize in Ferdinand a ruler who never mistook power for license.
He reminds us—fittingly, for a saint whose name marks a Missouri parish he never saw—that sanctity travels in strange and unpredictable directions across both centuries and oceans.
